title: Pir Budhu Shah
hook: a Sufi who sent his sons and followers to fight beside the Guru at Bhangani, where two sons fell

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirpa Ram of Kashmir, the pandit who came asking for help and, tradition says, came back years later to serve. Your line: he came back to serve. Today, a friend from another faith.

A recommendation can be a heavy thing to give. You put your name next to someone else's, and if they let the other person down, part of that is on you. Now raise the stakes. A holy man of one faith vouches for a band of soldiers to a teacher of another faith. The soldiers take the pay. Then, on the eve of a battle, most of them walk away. The holy man could send an apology. He could stay home. Instead, tradition says, he gathers his own sons and his own followers and rides toward the fighting. Today: Bhangani.
screen: `HE VOUCHED FOR THEM.` → `THEY WALKED AWAY.` → `HE RODE IN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Pir Budhu Shah was a Sufi, a Muslim teacher of the inner path, who lived at Sadhaura, not far from where the young Guru Gobind Singh was staying in the hills. Pir is a title for a spiritual guide. Tradition says the two men met and respected each other, and that the Pir recommended a company of Pathan soldiers who needed work. The Guru took them on. Then came Bhangani, the battle where hill rajas marched against him. Tradition says most of those Pathans deserted before the fighting, and only a few stayed. The Pir did not send excuses. He came himself, with his sons and his followers, to stand beside the Guru. And in that fighting, tradition says, two of his sons were killed. A father of one faith lost two sons defending a teacher of another, because, the story says, his word had been given. Afterward, the story goes, the Guru wanted to honor him. Tradition says the Pir asked for the comb the Guru had just used, with strands of his hair still caught in it, and the Guru gave it to him, along with a turban. Not land, not gold: just a comb. Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah with love. His story is told when people ask what friendship between faiths can look like. Not a polite handshake. Keeping your word when it costs you, beside someone who prays differently. And it reminds Sikhs that among the people around the Gurus were Muslims who gave everything.
screen: `A SUFI OF SADHAURA.` · `THE SOLDIERS HE VOUCHED FOR LEFT.` · `TWO SONS FELL AT BHANGANI.` · `HE ASKED ONLY FOR A COMB.` · then, large: `A SUFI'S SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone outside your own circle, another faith, another background, even a stranger, who once gave something up for you or for people you love. Let yourself remember what it cost them. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.
Bhangani, the battle where Pir Budhu Shah's sons died fighting beside Guru Gobind Singh after the soldiers he had vouched for deserted.
Your line: a sufi's sacrifice. His word held, all the way to Bhangani. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah in tellings of the battle of Bhangani and in talks and kirtan programs about the Muslims who stood with the Gurus, and his town of Sadhaura is remembered in that story.

chat.says: Who was Pir Budhu Shah, and why do Sikhs remember him so warmly?

A Muslim general paid by the Guru, who led the Pathans to victory at Bhangani.
A Sufi who sent soldiers to the Guru, then stayed home when they ran away.
